title: Maximum Fruits in K Steps
statement:
A grid has `r` rows and `c` columns. The value `g[i][j]` is the number of fruits you harvest each time you stand on cell `(i, j)`. You start on the cell `(sr, sc)` and may make **at most `k` moves**. In one move you step to one of the four neighbouring cells (up, down, left, right) without leaving the grid.

You harvest the fruits of your starting cell when you begin, and the fruits of every cell you step onto afterwards. Cells regrow instantly, so if you walk over the same cell again you harvest its fruits again.

Find the maximum total number of fruits you can harvest.

For example, in the grid `[[1,2,4,8],[3,0,2,1],[1,2,4,9]]` starting at the top-left cell with `k = 3`, walking right along the top row collects `1 + 2 + 4 + 8`.

**Follow-up:** what changes if the fruits of a cell can be harvested only once? Explain why the dynamic programming over (steps left, cell) no longer works directly.
inputFormat:
The first line contains `r` and `c`.
Each of the next `r` lines contains `c` integers: the grid `g`.
The last line contains `sr`, `sc` and `k` (0-indexed start row, start column, and the maximum number of moves).
outputFormat: Print a single integer: the maximum number of fruits that can be harvested.

examples.explanation: Walk right along the top row: start on 1, then step onto 2, 4 and 8, for 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15. Going down first (3, then 1) collects less.
Start on 4, step right onto 9, then step back onto 4 again, which regrows: 4 + 9 + 4 = 17.
There is nowhere to move, so only the starting cell is harvested.

hints: Let best[t][i][j] be the most fruits you can have collected after exactly t moves while standing on (i, j).
best[t][i][j] = g[i][j] + the maximum of best[t − 1] over the four neighbours of (i, j) that are reachable. Start with best[0][sr][sc] = g[sr][sc].
Because you may stop early, the answer is the maximum value seen over all t ≤ k and all cells. Only the previous layer is needed, so memory is O(r · c).
